newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin calls for purge of bad factory bosses.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin calls for purge of bad factory bosses.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin turned his heavy guns on Russia's factory directors on Friday, telling workers they should not tolerate corrupt and incompetent bosses.
Trying to defuse the pent-up frustrations of millions of state workers owed wages from as long as 14 months ago, Yeltsin said the factory directors were largely to blame.
"Unfortunately, there are many directors who have adapted to the market in a crafty way, turning the factory into their own feeding trough," he said in a nationwide radio address.
"They understand the market as the right to uncontrolled pumping of the factory's profit into their own fake companies, including those abroad."

Yeltsin reshuffled his government in March, blaming ministers for a policy hiatus and economic slide during his absence last year with heart problems. His return to the Kremlin with renewed vigour has been accompanied by weekly radio addresses, an idea developed by his daughter Tatyana.
The new, reformist cabinet this week promised to pay off public sector wage arrears by the end of the year. But the pledge has not stopped a new wave of protests.

The president hit back by saying the state owed just 20 percent of the debt. Bad directors were responsible for the remainder, he said, telling workers to use the shares they had received under market reforms to get rid of bad directors.
"There's no need to be afraid," he told them.
While Yeltsin, on holiday in the northwestern Karelia region, used the radio address to defend the government, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin took the message to a key region.

Chernomyrdin said his visit to a nuclear research centre in the reformist Nizhny Novgorod region had nothing to do with an election due there on Sunday, but the government is clearly worried wage delays could mean a vote against the government.
Yeltsin had promised to pay public sector wage arrears by October 1, but his ministers said they did not have the funds. On Tuesday he decreed the deadline would be January 1 next year.

Workers in towns and coal mines grouped around the Siberian coal centre Kemerovo, who had backed Yeltsin when he was fighting Soviet leaders, have now turned against him, including political demands in a new wave of wage protests.
"The Kemerovo proletariat, which threw its weight behind Boris Yeltsin (in 1991) is now demanding that Yeltsin and his team resign," wrote the opposition daily Nezavisimaya Gazeta.
But Yeltsin said it was the directors who had to go.

Acknowledging that few factories had been touched by bankruptcy procedures he told workers to use them to get better managers, of whatever political hue. "Let him be red, brown even striped, it doesn't matter. As long as a director can manage."
Looking ahead, Yeltsin said he had asked First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov to draw up a programme to train promising young Russians to lead the revival of Russian industry.
They would be sent abroad to learn from successful companies while Russians already working in other countries would be encouraged to bring their newly-acquired expertise back home.

"When our shops are flooded with imports, it makes you think, what about our factories, which are turning out the same refrigerators and raincoats, frying pans and vacuum cleaners, boots and toys?" Yeltsin said. "Where are their products going?"
